subtype: Approach: avoiding the conversation hoping it improves [Pitfall]
passage: Pallavi was twenty-six and Hansa, her junior on the team, was thirty-four. Whenever Hansa's reports came in with figures missing, Pallavi's stomach knotted at the thought of correcting someone who had been working since Pallavi was in school. "I'll mention it after festival week," she told herself. Then after the quarter-end. Then after Hansa's birthday. Four months went by with the small comments never made. At the annual review, the manager asked for examples, and Pallavi handed over a long list. Hansa read it, blinked, and said quietly, "Why didn't you tell me in March?" The room in the Pune office felt very small.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi keep postponing the feedback?
qa.a: Pallavi felt awkward about correcting someone older, and her stomach knotted at the thought.

qa.q: What could Pallavi have done in March, and why?
qa.a: Pallavi could have mentioned the missing figures in a short, kind chat when they first appeared, because small feedback early does not turn into a surprise later.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt reading the list at the review?
qa.a: Hansa was probably surprised and hurt, wondering why nobody had said anything for months.

grounding: Illustrates a lead feeling awkward about a junior being older and postponing feedback for months, so the review feels like a surprise.

"Avni, Nilesh's quarterly review is tomorrow. Have you talked to him about the reports?"
Avni stared at her screen. "Not really, Manoj."
"It's been four months."
"I know. He's fifteen years older than me. He's got kids in college. Every time I try, he calls me 'beta' and I lose my nerve."
"So he doesn't know."
"He knows the reports are late. He doesn't know it's serious."
The next afternoon, in the review room:
"Nilesh-ji, the rating this quarter is 'needs improvement'. The client reports were late in eleven weeks out of sixteen."
Nilesh put his pen down. "Eleven? Why didn't anyone tell me?"
"I... I should have."
"If I'd known in April, I could have fixed this. Now it's on my record." He looked more hurt than angry.
Avni's face burned. She had spared herself four awkward conversations and handed him one terrible one.

qa.q: How many weeks were the client reports late?
Why did Avni keep postponing the conversation?
qa.a: She felt awkward and nervous because Nilesh is fifteen years older and calls her 'beta', so she kept losing her nerve.

qa.q: What could Avni have done differently back in April?
qa.a: She could have given Nilesh specific, private feedback about the late reports as soon as they started, with a simple plan and check-ins.

qa.q: How does the review feel to Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh feels hurt and blindsided, because he learns about a serious problem only when it is already on his record.

grounding: It shows a lead who felt awkward about a junior being older than her postponing feedback for months, so the review comes as a surprise.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the conversation hoping it improves [Pitfall]
passage:
The hardest review I ever gave was one I had set up myself, months earlier, by saying nothing.
Ayesha joined my design team last year. She had worked in print for twenty years before switching to digital; I was twenty-five and had been a lead for eight months. When her screens came in off-grid or late, I'd think, who am I to tell someone her age? I'd fix them myself and smile at her in the corridor.
By October, the gaps had piled up: missed specs, three redesigns redone. The review form forced me to write "below expectations".
Ayesha read it and went very still. "Himani, I had no idea. You always said things looked fine."
I had. I had said that, to avoid feeling embarrassed.
She wasn't angry, just stunned. I was the one who couldn't look up.

qa.q: How many years had Ayesha worked in print?
Why did Himani keep telling Ayesha that things looked fine?
qa.a: Himani felt awkward and embarrassed giving feedback to someone much older and more experienced, so saying nothing felt easier at the time.

qa.q: What would you change first in Himani's approach?
qa.a: Give Ayesha specific, kind feedback on the first off-grid or late screens, privately and early, instead of quietly fixing them.

qa.q: How did the review feel to Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha was stunned, because months of "looks fine" had left her no chance to improve before the rating.

grounding: It shows a young lead, uneasy about a junior being older, postponing feedback for months so the review feels like a surprise.
